catalog_locator: Routamaa & Routamaa 1995: sec. 5.3 'Stress' p.16 through sec. 5.3.6 'Summary of stress' p.20; sec. 5.1 'Pitch/tone' p.14; sec. 5.2 'Vowel Length' pp.14-15; sec. 5.4 'Consonant Clusters' p.21. Routamaa & Routamaa 1997: sec. 3.2.1 'Stress and Tone' p.6.
catalog_quote: Kamula nouns generally have stress on the penultimate syllable. Stress manifests itself as a combination of vowel length, loudness and often, high tone. Many words in Kamula have no stress at all. To date, only a few words have been found that contrast stress, and so we propose that stress is not a contrastive feature of the language. Below is an exhaustive list to date. [p.16] ... The great majority of two-syllable nouns have stress on the first (ie. penultimate) syllable. [p.16] ... Three syllable nouns fall into two main categories: 1. Stress on the penultimate syllable 2. No stress at all. [p.17] ... The most common pattern for four syllable nouns is that the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. [p.19] ... The general tendency for five and six syllable nouns is to have the stress on the penultimate syllable. [p.19] ... Stress on verbs differs from stress on nouns in that stress, if it exists, most often falls on the first syllable of the verb stem, which is often the first syllable of the word. [p.20] ... As a general rule for nouns, stress, if it occurs, falls on the penultimate syllable. For verbs, if stress occurs, it generally falls on the first syllable of the verb stem. [p.20]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nouns of any length (2 to 6 syllables) are stressed on the penultimate syllable if they carry stress at all; verbs, if stressed, take stress on the first syllable of the verb stem (prefixes never take it). Stress is realised as vowel length plus loudness and usually high tone, is not contrastive apart from a handful of disyllabic pairs, and a sizeable class of nouns and verbs is described as having no stressed syllable at all. Kamula also has a marginal three-way tone contrast (high, low, low-high rise) independent of stress; length is conditioned by stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; no secondary stress is transcribed in any example (long words such as /tutukulamu/ [tutukuˈlaːmu] show a single stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is proposed to be non-contrastive but 6 words (3 disyllabic minimal pairs, e.g. /sala/ [saˈlaː] 'wife's younger sibling' vs [ˈsaːla] 'song') contrast penultimate vs final stress (p.16, ex.16); a handful of disyllables have high tone on the first syllable and stress on the second (ex.19, /sipe/ [síˈpèː]); 'Many words in Kamula have no stress at all' (p.16), including some disyllabic nouns (ex.20), a whole class of trisyllabic nouns with equal length/loudness (5.3.2.2 p.18) and many verbs (ex.31, p.20); a few trisyllables have initial stress (/mɔsesi/ [ˈmɔːsesi] 'wind', ex.23 p.19); 4-syllable words with stress on the 2nd syllable whose penultimate vowel is extra-short so they sound like penult-stressed trisyllables (ex.25 p.19); verbs: stress on the first syllable of the stem, not the prefix, except that a non-initial V-syllable in the stem takes it (ex.29-30, p.20).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, on citation forms of nouns and verbs (elicited lexical items and text material from Kesiki village, 1991-94), with CECIL instrumental traces of length, loudness and pitch; stress is realised as vowel length + loudness + often high tone; a tone system (high, low, low-high rise) exists with 9 listed minimal pairs and works independently of stress (p.14, p.16); phrase-final vowels 'taper off' and are excluded from the measurements (p.15).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kamula (kamu1260, ISO xla) as spoken in Kesiki (Wawoi Falls), Samokopa and Wasapea, Western Province; data collected 1991-94 chiefly in Kesiki; the authors state there are no dialect differences (1995: 2), confirmed by the 1996 dialect survey as reported in Suter & Usher 2017: 108. No differently named variety involved.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate) and the same document as the existing statement. It qualifies the rule: penult holds for nouns only, verbs are stem-initial, many words are unstressed, stress is proposed non-contrastive, and three lexical tones exist with few minimal pairs.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nouns: stress, when present, falls on the penultimate syllable (shown for 2-, 3-, 4-, 5- and 6-syllable nouns); stress is realised as vowel length + loudness + usually high tone, and vowel length is entirely conditioned by stress. Verbs: stress, when present, falls on the first syllable of the verb stem (prefixes never take it). Many nouns and verbs have no stress at all (all syllables equal in length and loudness). Only six words (three pairs) contrast stress, so the authors propose stress is not contrastive. Three tones (high, low, low-high rise) exist with a handful of minimal pairs and operate independently of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only one stressed syllable per word is ever transcribed (e.g. /wɔtakiliɛpa/ [wɔtakiliˈɛːpa] 'dragonfly', p.20).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) A handful of two-syllable nouns with final stress, some with high tone on the first syllable: /sipe/ [síˈpèː], /mate/ [máˈtèː], /bati/ [báˈtìː], /bokɛ/, /wokɛ/, and the stress minimal pairs /sala/ 'wife's younger sibling' vs 'song', /aja/ 'older sister's child' vs 'house', /awa/ (pp.16-17); (b) many 2- and 3-syllable nouns with no stress at all (/doko/, /hema/, /dupa/, /bapo/; /alila/, /kapala/, /tekele/ etc., pp.17-18); (c) a few 3-syllable nouns with initial stress: /mɔsesi/ [ˈmɔːsesi] 'wind', /mɛsoso/ 'kind of tree' (p.19); (d) 4-syllable nouns with stress on the second syllable whose penult vowel becomes extra short so they sound penult-stressed (/aijakolo/ [aiˈjaːkŏlo] 'jaw', /omapela/ 'sky', p.19), likewise some 5-syllable nouns (p.20); (e) verbs: a non-stem-initial V-syllable in the stem takes the stress (/hutiɛma/ [hutiˈɛːma]), prefixed verbs keep stem stress (/potasema/ [poˈtaːsəma]), and many verbs are unstressed (/hama/, /tima/, p.20). Sec. 5.1 p.14: 'There are few traces of tone in Kamula.. There are three different types of tone: high, low and low-high rise' with 9 minimal pairs.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe the Kamula of the Wawoi Falls / Kesiki area (Routamaa 1994 p.7 reports ~800 speakers in three villages with no dialect differences). No work in the list describes another variety or language.
